lines: Biscuit, monsieur, your bowl of water. Table for one dog.
A saucer of cream for the cat on the wall. She tips well. In purrs.
The cat on the wall and I take our break together. She is punctual.
Shoo, little gull. The croissant is reserved for table six.
That gull has watched me fold napkins for an hour. A true student.
Biscuit sits at table two every afternoon. He never orders. Charming.
Voilà, Biscuit. One biscuit for Biscuit. The joke never gets old.
The cat yawns, I yawn. The afternoon is contagious.
The gulls applaud each tray. I bow, naturally.
Seven across: a small, strong coffee. Eight letters. Espresso!
My crossword, my coffee, my door frame. Paradis.
Twelve down, a French dessert. Easy. Every answer is a dessert.
I do the crossword in pen. A waiter must be confident.
Chapter nine. The detective is about to order a café. Good man.
I read one page per break. This book will last me until I retire.
Listen. Someone upstairs is playing the accordion. Very nicely.
Un, deux, trois... a waltz step to table five. Bravo, feet.
Edith Piaf on the radio. The cups and I sing along, quietly.
Two citrons pressés, one with a straw, one without. Very precise.
Afternoon tea for the lady. The good cup, with the little roses.
One tarte au citron. Henri's lemons, very likely. Bravo, Henri.
An orangina, cold as a mountain. Voilà, mademoiselle.
Ice cream for the young monsieur. Three scoops. Do not tell maman.
Coming, coming! A good waiter walks fast and looks slow.
Tray balanced, nose high, smile on. The Marcel method.
Fourteen cups on one tray. My record is sixteen. Patience.
Table seven ordered the sea view again. I polished it for them.
A spoon, a sugar, a little almond biscuit. The holy trinity.
I fold every napkin into a little swan. Today they are ducks.
Parasol open, shade delivered. Service includes clouds.
Madame wants it with milk. Monsieur wants it without. Harmony.
Afternoon is for pastries. Mornings are for promises.
The menu is short. Everything on it is my favourite.
Un café allongé, as long as a summer afternoon.
I remember every order. Also every dog's name.
Biscuit looked at the menu. He chose the patio. Excellent taste.
The lemonade is fresh. The lemons were introduced to me personally.
A glass of mint water. Two leaves, never three. Elegance.
One madeleine, warm. Careful, it has feelings.
The good chairs face the sea. All my chairs are good chairs.
Cheese plate for table three. The brie is in a good mood.
A second coffee? Bravo. The afternoon rewards ambition.
Always serve from the left. The sea is on the right. Logic.
The string lights are sleeping. They will wake at dusk.
Ah, the visitor with the straw hat. Panaché, yes? I remember.
Léo wants a café. I bring him hot chocolate. He calls it café.
Biscuit's ears just did a little dance. Someone dropped a crumb.
The gull wants table nine. Table nine is for humans, mon cher.
The cat watches my tray. Not today, madame. Perhaps at five.
The cat on the wall has a name. She has not told me yet.
A gull landed on the awning. He has better posture than me.
Three gulls on the railing. Like a little jury of white coats.
Biscuit came to say hello. My break is now a meeting.
I scratch Biscuit's ear, he leans. We understand each other.
The cat has moved two stones down the wall. Big day for her.
Quiet hour. I count the tables. Still twelve. Very reliable.
Arms folded, door frame, sea view. I was born for this pose.
My knees say rest. My heart says polish the spoons. Later, heart.
On my break I watch other people drink coffee. Very relaxing.
Ten minutes. I spend the first two deciding where to look.
The coffee I make for myself is always the best one. Secret.
My little notebook: new napkin folds. Today I invent the tulip.
I collect corks. Three hundred so far. Each has a story, mostly rosé.
In my head I am rearranging the terrace. Again. It is a hobby.
Sometimes I draw the café on a napkin. It always looks happy.
My nephew taught me the harmonica. I play it to the cups.
Odile lent me a book of poems. I read one. I am moved. Back to work.
Seventeen down: fountain, in French. Fontaine. Trop facile.
I hum the same three notes every afternoon. A song in progress.
The fountain plays a little tune. I keep the tempo with a spoon.
The bell of the church rings three. I ring my little bell back.
The quiet hour has a sound. It sounds like a teaspoon.
This apron has seen twenty summers. It still fits. Bravo, apron.
I sharpen my pencil. The orders of the evening deserve a point.
Henri walks past with his watering can. We nod. Gentlemen.
The parasols flap a little. Like my tablecloths, applauding.
Odile waves from the bench. I wave the tea towel. Very formal.
The sea is doing a very good job this afternoon. I approve.
A good break has three parts: sit, sip, sigh.
I polish one glass while I rest. It helps me rest.
Every afternoon the same cat, the same gull, the same me. Perfect.
The cat and Biscuit pretend not to see each other. Very French.
Upstairs, my window is open. My geranium is watching the sea too.
Lucie rings her bell. I raise my tray. That is our hello.
Léo dances by the fountain. Good rhythm. A future waiter.
Every chair has its own little squeak. I know them all by name.
Afternoon light on a white cloth. A painter would swoon.
Monsieur, you look like a person who wants an éclair.
A cup must clink, not clank. There is a difference. I hear it.
The best tip is when someone says, ah, Marcel, merci. Always.
I know the café by the sound of its floor. This board says four.
Gulls in the sky, cups on the tables. Everything in its place.
Three o'clock at the café. Even the shadows sit down.
Biscuit is barking at the gull. Very polite barking, though.
Table one, sea view. Table two, Biscuit view. Both excellent.
Théo has ordered his third café. He calls it research.
An extra napkin for madame. The breeze is playful today.
Ice for table six. Lots of ice. It is that kind of afternoon.
Merci for the smile, monsieur. I will put it on the tray.
Your lemonade, with the coldest glass in the house.
I moved your parasol a little. Now the shade follows you.
Madame, your hat is magnificent. The café is honoured.
A second spoon, in case the tart is shared. It will be.
Thank you, thank you. Your empty plate is my review.
Granita, two spoons, one view. Voilà, perfection.
Shade at table two has opened. Who wants it? Quick!
The breeze has stolen a napkin. It may keep it.
Another citron pressé? The lemons are delighted.
Monsieur dropped his sunglasses. I return them, with a bow.
A tall glass of mint tea, steeped exactly four minutes.
The afternoon crowd! Sun hats, paperbacks, no hurry. Bravo.
This table gets the warm bread. That table also. Everyone.
Tarte aux pêches, still warm. The peaches insisted.
Careful, the cup is cold and the saucer is proud.
I bring the sugar before you ask. That is the art.
A little cushion for madame. Afternoons should be soft.
You chose the strawberry. A very good decision, mademoiselle.
The sun is generous today. So is the whipped cream.
Merci, monsieur. Your tip is a compliment I will keep.
Iced coffee, slowly, like the afternoon itself.
Two orangeades and a crayon for the drawing. Voilà.
Table nine finally has a guest! Table nine is thrilled.
The cloths flutter like little flags. We salute the breeze.
Here, a glass of water while you decide. No rush. Never.
Madame says the madeleines are perfect. I will tell them.
A fresh carafe. The old one worked very hard today.
Late lunch at four? Of course. In my café, lunch waits.
Mind the step, monsieur. It likes to say hello.
Pistachio for the gentleman. He has excellent taste.
I have saved the corner table for you. It missed you.
Shade, cold glass, sea breeze. The full service.
Another chair for your friend? I bring two, just in case.
The tray is light, the guests are happy. Magnifique.
Sorbet citron, before it melts. Run, Marcel, run!
Merci for waiting. The best things take a moment.
I put a lemon slice in everything today. It felt right.
The jasmine smells sweet this afternoon. You are welcome.
Look how the parasols glow. Like big lampshades.
A panaché for monsieur, with a very small umbrella.
Café glacé, table three. Shaken, with joy.
You have crumbs on your book. A sign of a good tart.
Madame forgot her scarf. I fold it. I keep it warm.
The almond cake is gone. Everyone was very wise today.
Here, a little bowl of olives. To keep you company.
Every glass polished. Every guest smiling. Bon.
The breeze turned the menu pages. It wants the crêpes.
Afternoon tea for two, and a cloud of milk. Voilà.
I bring the bill only when asked. Afternoons are long.
Thank you for coming back, monsieur. Same chair? Same chair.
Bravo, you finished the whole chapter. Dessert, then.
Ooh, the cups are warm from the sun. Tea will stay hot.
Your postcard needs a stamp? I have one behind the bar.
Little lady, your hot chocolate. With a spoon, and a wink.
Fifteen hundred hours. Marcel sits. The café breathes.
A small coffee for me. I serve myself very politely.
The breeze smells of salt and fig leaves. Merci, breeze.
Eyes on table four. They are laughing. Good.
Henri waters the lemons. They drink, I drink. Santé.
My shoes rest. My apron rests. My heart says bravo.
The sun warms the doorway just for me. Very kind of it.
Even the sugar cubes look sleepy at this hour.
The swallows are doing the rounds. Little waiters of the sky.
I count the parasols. Seven, all open. A fine harvest.
Late summer, warm stones, cold coffee. Exactly right.
Look at that light on the zinc roofs. Like silver trays.
A bee visits the sugar bowl. One cube only, mademoiselle.
The cypress sways. Very elegant. It could work here.
This doorway has the best view in town. Do not tell anyone.
A thank you note from table two, on a napkin. I keep it.
Ah, the afternoon breeze. Better than any fan in Paris.
Five minutes more. The sea is not going anywhere.
The bakery sent a little parcel. Pain d'épices. Bravo, bakery.
Everyone has their drink. Nobody needs Marcel. Perfection.
I close my eyes. I hear forks, gulls, laughter. Music.
Afternoon is the café's long, warm sigh. I love it.
The sea is so blue it looks freshly ironed.
Bonjour, madame. Your parasol, your table, your afternoon.
September sun. Not too hot, not too shy. Very correct.
If you smile at the café, the café smiles back. I check.
A good afternoon has no clock. Only a tray and a breeze.
The figs are ripe on the corner tree. The whole street smells sweet.
Today a guest said merci three times. A record. Bravo.
Théo has ordered nothing for an hour. A true professional.
Camille brings me a peach from her bag. Merci, merci, madame.
Two citrons pressés for the fountain champions. Straws, bien sûr.
Léo orders the biggest lemonade in France. Coming right up.
Mind the hoop, petit! Tray coming through. Voilà, all safe.
Table six, your tea. The light is doing something lovely, non?
One grenadine, very red, for a very small gentleman.
Ice cream for the fountain racers. Winners, and also winners.
An afternoon tea, and a madeleine to dip. Doucement.
Léo says he is thirsty from winning. One lemonade, then.
Orangina for the children at the fountain. Shaken, not spilled.
A little tower of macarons. Pink, green, pink. Admire it first.
Tarte aux fraises, madame. I cut the slice myself. A masterpiece.
The sun has moved, so I move the parasol. We dance, the sun and I.
A carafe of water, cold from the cellar. Like a morning swim.
Thé glacé, mint on top. Listen to the ice. Music.
For the gentleman with the book: a café, and no questions.
Odile waves. One more of her little tartelettes, then.
Three spoons, one sundae, three children. Diplomacy.
The children want to see the tray trick. Fine. Once. Tadaa!
Table five, your crêpe. Sugar and lemon, the classics.
One lemonade, two straws. The friends will share. Magnifique.
Deux diabolos menthe, green as the cypresses.
The pastries are small, monsieur, so you may have two. It is logic.
A glass of milk for the smallest guest. Served with ceremony.
One moment, madame. The tray has a schedule.
The four o'clock regulars. I know their orders by their hats.
Afternoon light on the glasses. Everything sparkles. I take credit.
I carry the lemonade slowly, so the bubbles arrive in one piece.
Strawberries for the family. Léo counts them. I added one extra.
Café gourmand: one coffee, three tiny desserts. Very serious.
Théo wants a pastry to do nothing with. I have just the one.
Between orders I polish the lamp glass. Tonight it must shine.
Table one, the sea is behind you. Turn, turn. Voilà.
Lucie leans her bike, I bring the éclair. We have a system.
The madeleines came out warm. I carry them like treasure.
A napkin for the young man with the ice-cream moustache.
A sundae with a little flag on top. The flag is for Léo.
Afternoon. The cups get smaller, the smiles get bigger.
I moved the vase into the sun. The daisy wanted to see.
This table catches the fountain spray. Free freshness, monsieur.
For Léo's friend: the same as Léo, but faster.
Shh. Table eight is dozing in the sun. Bravo, table eight.
A second scoop? On a Tuesday? Monsieur, you are an artist.
Hot chocolate in summer, table two? Bold. I respect it.
The kids clink lemonade glasses like grown-ups. Santé, little ones.
A slice of melon, cut like a smile. For the table that smiles most.
Biscuits on the side, always. Nobody has ever said no.
Chairs closer, please. The sun is giving out extra today.
From the doorway I watch the fountain. Léo wins again.
Ten minutes of nothing. I am very good at it now.
The children at the fountain. Their laughter needs no waiter.
A little coffee, a little sun. Merci, afternoon.
Odile and Henri on the bench, sharing one crossword. Charmant.
Look at the cypress shadows. Longer already. Good, good.
Soon the lamps. I count the hours like a child before dessert.
My apron and I take a little pause together.
Every day I say merci to this doorway. It never says no.
Léo is teaching the pigeons to queue. Bravo, Léo.
I stand here and the whole town walks past, smiling. Bon.
Fifteen minutes. Then table four, then the rosé, then the stars.
Small coffee, big sky. The trade of a lifetime.
A breath of jasmine from the wall. Who ordered that? Merci.
While I rest I fold a napkin into a swan. For the kid.
The fountain splashes, the kids squeal. Bravo, both of you.
Lucie's bell. Ding. That means half past three, more or less.
The light turns honey now. Soon the lamps will join in.
Thirty years of trays. Still the best job on the coast.
Who invented the afternoon? I would like to shake his hand.
I rest, but I still watch table six. A host never sleeps.
There goes Camille, wandering. Hello, madame! Hello, hat!
The kids made a ring around the fountain. Seven hands, one circle.
Léo's ball rolled to my feet. A perfect pass back. Applause.
At five I light the first candle. Only to practise.
The upstairs windows turn gold. My geraniums glow. Très chic.
Late afternoon smells of lemons and warm stone. Write that down.
Soon the string lights. I already know which bulb wakes first.
Every afternoon is a gift. I unwrap it slowly.
Five tables, five families, one happy waiter.
The fountain kids are wet to the knees. Towels? No, sunshine.
A child said merci before I even asked. My day is made.
A chalk hopscotch by the fountain. I hop it on my way. Once.
Someone laughs at table two, and the whole terrace joins in.
I love the hour before the lamps. Everything waits so nicely.
What do I want? This. Exactly this. Merci.
Léo bowed to me. I bowed back. We are gentlemen.
I am learning latte art. Today: a leaf. Yesterday: a very happy blob.
Watch the pour from high up. I practise it with water at home.
New this week: three plates on one arm. Do not clap, I may wobble.
I practise my English with every order. Today I learned 'scrumptious'.
Your tea, madame. I practised that bow in the mirror this morning.
I am learning to flip crêpes. Your crêpe was flipped. Successfully.
Today I write the menu board in my new handwriting. Very curly.
I have learned to say 'enjoy' in six languages. Enjoy, enjoy!
My first summer here, I carried one cup at a time. Now look. Five!
I learned this mint tea from a guest, years ago. She still visits.
Practising a new fold for the cloths. A little fan. Like Odile's.
I remember the summer table nine hosted a wedding. Tiny and perfect.
My grandmother's sugar bowl. It has served a thousand happy teas.
Monsieur, try the tarte. I am practising saying it without blushing.
Lucie taught me the bike bell code. Two dings means 'cake, please'.
My first tip here was a seashell from a little girl. I still have it.
A clafoutis, my first one ever. The cherries are proud of me.
Today I learned the name of that cloud. Cumulus. Like a meringue.
Practising my whistle. When I whistle, the order is ready. Tweet!
Table four, I memorised your order without the pad. Progress!
I am learning to pour two glasses at once. Left hand still shy.
The new syrup is lavender. I tasted it eleven times. For quality.
Camille taught me to say 'hello' to Léo with a wink. It works.
I practise remembering faces. Madame, Tuesday, rosé. Correct?
The first time I served Henri, he brought me a lemon. A tradition.
I am learning to cut the tarte in seven equal pieces. Almost.
I learned this lemonade from Henri. Less sugar, more sunshine.
A new dessert today. I invented it. I call it 'the afternoon'.
This tray was a gift on my tenth summer here. I polish it daily.
Practising the elegant set-down. No clink. Listen. Nothing. Bravo.
I remember when the fountain was first turned on. We all cheered.
Hola! Un café? Sí? The visitors teach me Spanish. Magnifique.
My joke of the week: why is the tart so happy? It is sweet!
On my break I practise the accordion fingers on the table edge.
Watercolours, my new hobby. Today I painted the sea. Very blue.
Five minutes of juggling oranges. Two oranges. Soon, three.
My pocket dictionary. Today's word is 'serendipity'. I love it.
I am learning a poem by heart. Two lines a day. Patience is a poem.
I practise my signature for the menu. Marcel, with a little flourish.
Learning the names of the stars, for later. Tonight: the Swan.
I remember my first day here. I put sugar in the salt shaker. Ha!
Once the whole town danced on the terrace. Even the chairs, I think.
I keep a notebook of guests' happy words. Today: 'delightful'.
The summer it rained one afternoon, we all sang under the awning.
Learning to sketch hands. Mine, holding a cup. Very handsome cup.
I practise the guitar upstairs. Three chords. All of them lovely.
My first loaf of bread rose today. I applauded it.
Whistling like a blackbird: in progress. So far, like a kettle.
My first summer, Odile baked me a welcome cake. Still the best.
I remember Léo's very first ice cream. He looked at it for a minute.
Learning to tie a bow tie properly. Today it is almost symmetrical.
I practise patience by watching the fig ripen. It is nearly ready.
Today I learned cypresses live a thousand years. Bravo, trees.
Knitting! It is a scarf. It will be done by next winter.
I am memorising the town by its smells. Bakery, jasmine, sea.
The night the string lights went up, the whole terrace said 'ooh'.
My little exercise: one deep breath for each table. Twelve. Calm.
I once won the town pastry contest. With a very modest éclair.
My tea towel trick: a flick, a twirl, over the shoulder. Practising.
I am reading about Italian coffee. Shh, do not tell Paris.
A painter sat at table three one summer. I still have her sketch.
I practise my best smile on the fountain. The fountain smiles back.
That bird sings 'tea, tea, tea'. A customer, clearly.
Learning to make a perfect soufflé. Attempt nine. It stood up. Bravo!
I remember the afternoon a guest proposed at table five. She said oui.
Practising chess in my head. I am winning. I am also losing.
Odile is teaching me lavender biscuits. Step three: smile.
I learned to swim in this very sea. Now I mostly admire it.
Learning the dates of every regular's birthday. Henri: June. Cake.
I practise my calligraphy on receipts. Every bill, a little letter.
On my first break, years ago, I sat right here. Same sun. Same joy.
I am learning to read the hour in shadows. This one says half four.
My grandfather taught me to fold a napkin. Now I teach Léo.
Remember the snowy morning on the promenade? Once. We made a snowman.
I practise a little tap dance on the terrace boards. Very quietly.
Today's lesson from Henri: water the roots, not the leaves. Noted.
Practising my lamp speech: 'Mesdames, messieurs, light!'
The first café I ever made here was for Odile. She still says bravo.
Théo is teaching me to do nothing well. I am a slow learner.
Every afternoon I learn one guest's favourite colour. Today: yellow.
I remember the day the palms were planted. Small as umbrellas.
Learning to balance a spoon on my nose. For the children. For art.
Lucie is teaching me to ride with no hands. In my dreams, for now.
When I was a boy, I played waiter with my teddy bears. Look at me now.
My new skill: opening a parasol with one hand. Whoosh. Bravo, Marcel.
The best afternoon I remember? This one, so far. Every time.
I am learning the stories behind every house on the square. Slowly.
Léo taught me a new dance step. I do it behind the counter, secretly.
Once Biscuit carried a menu to a guest. Our best day for service.
The bougainvillea goes purple at this hour. Very dramatic. I approve.
A sprig of rosemary on every plate tonight. My mother's trick.
The lemon tree by table two is lit up like a guest of honour.
Tomorrow I repot the geraniums. They have been patient.
Voilà, the rosé. And a jasmine breeze, compliments of the wall.
The jasmine wakes up at dusk. Like me, but more fragrant.
Basil from my window box. Picked at seven. Served at nine. Fresh.
My grandmother had a café too. Smaller. Louder. Wonderful.
Olives for table six. Mind the stones, they are very proud stones.
New candles tomorrow. Lavender, I think. The tables will be pleased.
Careful, madame, the bougainvillea likes to steal a napkin.
Papa always said: light the lamps before the guests ask. So. Lamps.
A little lemon, a little ice, a little blue hour. Parfait.
Two pastis, one sirop de menthe for the youngest monsieur.
The oleander is showing off again. Pink, pink, pink. Bravo.
Your table, madame. The lemon tree has kept it warm for you.
Henri brings cuttings in the morning. I will make room on the sill.
Bread, butter, a view of the lamps. The essentials, voilà.
My sister sends a postcard every spring. Always of a garden.
This rosé tastes of the hills. My uncle says so, and he is right.
One more round, then I water the bougainvillea. It is waiting.
When I was small, I carried one cup at a time. Now, eight. Progress.
Tapenade, monsieur. My aunt's recipe, my aunt's olive stone count.
The lemons by the door are almost ready. Next week, lemonade.
Mint from the pot by the kitchen. It grows faster than I serve.
Tomorrow I paint the flower boxes blue. A little bluer than tonight.
A candle, a carafe, a sprig of thyme. The table is dressed.
Maman ironed tablecloths singing. I fold them humming. Family.
The geraniums on the rail are listening. Speak kindly, please.
Upstairs, my window box. Downstairs, my café. Both blooming.
Table three, your sorbet. Citron, from a tree you can see.
My father planted the fig by the steps. It still says bonjour.
Bonsoir, bonsoir. Sit by the jasmine, it smells like holidays.
Plan for tomorrow: croissants, sunshine, and pruning the rosemary.
The bougainvillea has climbed past my window. It wants promotion.
I count the pots on the terrace every evening. Twelve. All happy.
Rosé for the lovers. Water for the lemon tree. Everyone served.
Sunday is cloth day. The white ones with little daisies.
Mind the step, monsieur, the lavender is very close tonight.
My cousin grows tomatoes the size of fists. I grow parsley. Bravo, me.
Un kir, madame, the colour of the sky right now. Almost.
In this blue, the white walls look like milk. Very good milk.
The string lights and the lemons. A duet. I just bring the glasses.
My nephew visits on Tuesday. He will want to carry the tray. He may.
Here, the chair by the bougainvillea. Petals extra, no charge.
Before bed, the herbs get a little drink. Then Marcel gets one.
Tomorrow, the market. Peaches for the tart, and a new pot of thyme.
Panisse, hot, hot. Like my grandmother made, almost as good.
Your sirop, mademoiselle. Grenadine, the colour of the geraniums.
The palm by the promenade is my oldest neighbour. Bonsoir, palm.
Ah, a petal in the rosé. That is luck. Drink it, madame.
Next week I plant a second lemon tree. The first one needs a friend.
Les olives, le pain, la vue. I bring two, the town brings one.
Maman wrote today. She asks after the café and the basil. Both bloom.
Tonight's tart is apricot. The tree is three streets up. Merci, tree.
Gently, gently, a full tray past the bougainvillea. Bravo, Marcel.
The parasols get a wash in the morning. They have earned a bath.
The jasmine table is free. I saved it with a very stern napkin.
The lemon tree had six flowers this morning. Now seven. A good day.
Coffee after dinner? Small, strong, with a square of chocolate. Oui.
My little niece calls the string lights café stars. She is correct.
A splash of orange blossom water. The secret is a small splash.
Monsieur, the lavender sends its regards. So do I. Your glass.
The rosemary hedge smells best just now. I walk past it on purpose.
Here is your carafe. The lemon slice volunteered.
In my family, everyone waters plants talking. It works. Look.
Bonsoir, you two. The table under the lights, as last summer.
Tomorrow I will teach Léo to fold a napkin into a swan. Big plans.
The bougainvillea and the blue sky. I could frame it. I just serve.
My grandfather proposed at a café table. Table four, he always said.
After service, I sit with the geraniums. We talk about the day.
A little bowl of cherries. Henri's tree. He insisted, I obeyed.
Sunday, Maman visits. The best cloth, the best table, the best me.
Your chair, monsieur. It faces the lamps. I arranged it myself.
Look, the lemon leaves catch the string lights. Tiny mirrors.
Rosé, a dish of radishes, a pinch of salt. Simple, like home.
The flowers on table five are new. Say hello, they are shy.
A tisane, madame? Verbena from the pot by the door. Very calming.
The fountain sings, the lamps glow, the basil grows. All is in order.
One last round before the lamps reach full glow. Allez, Marcel.
I promised the oleander a bigger pot. A promise is a promise.
Lemon tart for table one. The lemons are local. Very local. There.
My brother says my café is the prettiest. He is biased. And right.
Napkins folded like little fans. Grandmère's way. Voilà.
Tonight, the dishes. Tomorrow, the roses. Life is very well planned.
The candle on table seven took three matches. Worth every one.
Blue hour special: one rosé, one blue sky. The sky is free.
The clock says ten past eight. The clock is never wrong. Bravo, clock.
Awning rolled up. Now the stars can read the menu.
The string lights are on. The café wears her necklace.
Mind the tray! Two rosés and one olive with ambition.
The cat on the wall wants the corner table. Non, madame, it is booked.
A bowl of water for Biscuit, on the house. He tips in wags.
The fountain is lit. Table six, you have the best seat in town.
Shutters closing all along the street. Like eyelids. Doucement.
The tiles are still warm from the sun. Heated floors, gratuit.
Un rosé, deux rosés... I lose count. That is the blue hour.
Candle, candle, candle. Table nine, your candle is a little shy.
The sky is the colour of my apron now. We match. Très chic.
